extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy; readers studying the theory of propositions, predication, and classification
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analytic criteria for understanding what propositions assert (the five kinds of matters-of-fact), the nature of verbal/essential vs real/accidental propositions, transformation between abstract and concrete terms, and the doctrine of the predicables (genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence as a matter-of-fact asserted by propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence is one of the five things that can be affirmed or denied in any proposition which is not merely verbal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every non-verbal proposition, when asserting something about a subject, may assert its existence (or non-existence). Treat 'existence' as a distinct kind of matter-of-fact to be detected when analyzing a proposition's import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-existence (Order in Place) as a matter-of-fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-existence (sometimes described more particularly as Order in Place) is another of the five exhaustive kinds of matters-of-fact that propositions may assert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when a proposition affirms that two or more attributes or phenomena concur spatially (arrangement in place with numerical intervals). Distinguish this from co-inherence of attributes (a different variety).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence / Order in Time as a matter-of-fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence (or Order in Time) is one of the five species of matter-of-fact asserted by non-verbal propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proposition asserts that one fact or phenomenon follows another in time, classify it under Sequence/Order in Time; this covers temporal order and is closely related to causation in some analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation as a matter-of-fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Causation is one of the five kinds of things which can be affirmed or denied in propositions that are not merely verbal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize propositions that assert causal relations as a separate category; in analysis, separate pure sequence (temporal order) from causation (where one fact brings about another).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance as a matter-of-fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Resemblance (simple likeness) is one of the five exhaustive kinds of matters-of-fact which propositions may assert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this category for predicates that convey mere likeness to other things or sensations (e.g., calling a sensation 'white' affirms resemblance to other 'white' sensations). The names of feelings often connote mere resemblance rather than analyzable attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Order in Place and Co-inherence of Attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Bain's distinction: one kind of co-existence accounts for Place (Order in Place), while another kind—co-inherence—refers to the concurrence of attributes or powers in the same part or locality (e.g., properties of gold, or mental functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat co-inherence as a distinct variety of co-existence often belonging to Time rather than Place; note that co-inherence sometimes refers to potential presence (attributes considered as existing even if not presently conscious). This distinction is important when classifying propositions about concurrent properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract terms convertible to concrete equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proposition expressed in abstract terms can be transformed into a precisely equivalent proposition using corresponding concrete terms (either names of the attributes themselves or the fundamenta of those attributes—the facts or phenomena on which they are grounded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For analysis, render abstract predicates into concrete statements about sensations, facts, or phenomena to clarify which of the five matters-of-fact is really asserted; e.g., 'Thoughtlessness is dangerous' -> 'Thoughtless actions are dangerous.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential (merely verbal) propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential propositions are purely verbal: they assert only what is asserted in the fact of calling a thing by a particular name (i.e., what is contained in the name's connotation) and so are not strictly truth-apt but conform to usage or convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize essential predication as giving no new information to one who already knows the full meaning of the terms. Their chief useful form is Definitions, which should, ideally, unfold the whole connotation of the name. Proof for such propositions is proof of usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-essential (accidental or real) propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-essential (accidental or real) propositions predicate of a thing some fact not involved in the signification of the name; these propositions, if true, add to our knowledge and are the proper subjects of inquiry and proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as the informative class of propositions; include individual-designation propositions and general propositions where the predicate connotes attributes not implied by the subject. These are the propositions that serve as data in reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the copula and implied existence
rubrics_metrics.description: The copula is ambiguous: besides marking predication it is a concrete word connoting existence, which can produce an implied assertion of real existence in many propositions (especially essential ones), though this implication arises from language imperfection rather than from logical necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a proposition implies existence, be aware that language may misleadingly suggest existence (e.g., 'A ghost is a disembodied spirit') even if the speaker doesn't believe in such entities; adjust analysis to separate linguistic implication from intended factual claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions as marks or evidence in practical reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewed as memoranda for practical use, a general proposition (e.g., 'All men are mortal') means that the attributes of the subject are a mark or evidence of the predicate (i.e., they indicate what to expect in an individual case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For purposes of reasoning, prefer the practical formula: read general propositions as prescribing which facts are evidential of others. This viewpoint is especially useful when using propositions as premises to support further inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrinal predicables: genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens
rubrics_metrics.description: The predicables are a fivefold division of general names (not grounded on difference in meaning but on the kind of class they denote): genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens. The same name may fall into different predicables depending on the subject of predication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the predicables to analyse relations between predicates and subjects in classification and definition. Remember they indicate relational role in predication (e.g., 'animal' is a genus relative to man, but a species relative to 'substance').

rubrics_metrics.name: General names create classes; classification arises from language
rubrics_metrics.description: Every significant name that connotes attributes potentially designates a class of objects possessing those attributes; classes mostly owe their existence to general language, though sometimes names are introduced to create convenient classes (as in natural history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming or evaluating classifications, recognize that names both express attributes and may be introduced for pragmatic grouping. The principles that ought to regulate classification for investigation will be considered further, but for analysis treat class membership as determined by connoted attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of sensations/feelings connote mere resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of simple sensations or feelings (e.g., 'white', 'tightness') are connotative but connote mere resemblance rather than analyzable attributes; predicating such class-names of an individual feeling conveys only likeness to previously named sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify predicate assertions about sensations as assertions of resemblance. For such predicates, the informative content is that the present sensation resembles prior sensations that bear the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential propositions in syllogistic examples are uninformative
rubrics_metrics.description: Many traditional syllogistic examples employ essential propositions (e.g., 'Every man is rational') which, being verbal, add no new knowledge beyond the meanings of terms and therefore give an exaggerated impression of syllogistic futility when used as paradigms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using merely essential propositions as primary examples when illustrating syllogistic or logical methods; prefer examples where the premises predicate attributes not already contained in the subject's name to demonstrate the utility of reasoning.
